intents.q: Set up a Flutter repository

cmds.n: Excludes .dart_tool, build, and generated platform files.
Commit the lockfile for applications so builds are reproducible; packages usually leave it out.

variants.undo: Remove the ignore file or untrack the lockfile

intents.q: Set up a Python repository

cmds.n: Excludes __pycache__, .venv, and build folders. Never commit the virtual environment: it is machine-specific and large.
Or pyproject.toml and the lockfile. Those describe the environment; the environment itself is rebuilt, not stored.

intents.q: Git settings for a PHP or Laravel project

cmds.n: Keeps vendor, node_modules, and the environment file out.
The lockfile pins dependencies; the example file documents the variables without their values.

intents.q: Version a LaTeX thesis or paper

cmds.n: Build artifacts regenerate; only the sources belong in history. Some authors commit the final PDF per release instead.
Prose diffs read far better word by word. One sentence per line in the source makes every diff surgical.

intents.q: Version a blog or static site

cmds.n: Commit content and configuration, never the generated output. For Jekyll, ignore _site and .jekyll-cache.
Let a workflow build and deploy, so the repository stays sources-only.

intents.q: Back up a notes vault with Git

cmds.n: Ignore per-machine workspace state and keep the notes and shared settings. Markdown diffs and merges cleanly.
A scheduled commit keeps a private repository as a versioned backup, with every past revision recoverable.

intents.q: Keep Kubernetes manifests in Git

cmds.n: The cluster's desired state lives in the repository; a controller like Argo CD or Flux reconciles the cluster to whatever main says. Rollback becomes git revert.
Plain Secrets must never be committed. Use sealed secrets or an external store and commit only the encrypted reference.

variants.undo: git revert the manifest commit and let the controller reconcile

intents.q: Move CI from Jenkins to GitHub Actions

cmds.n: Jenkins stages become jobs with needs:, agents become runs-on, and credentials become repository secrets. Shell steps usually port unchanged.
Where a job needs the old hardware, register that machine as a self-hosted runner and migrate the rest first.

variants.undo: Keep Jenkins running until the workflow proves itself

intents.q: Choose which repositories to show an employer

cmds.n: Depth beats breadth: three finished projects with clear READMEs, tests, and real commit history read better than thirty tutorials.
Reviewers do read history. Meaningful messages and steady commits say more about you than the star count.

intents.q: Teach Git to a class or a team

cmds.n: Teach the model before the commands: four places code lives, branches as labels, and the reflog as the safety net. Fear disappears once people know nothing committed is lost.
GitHub Classroom hands out template repositories and collects work as pull requests, which teaches the real workflow rather than a simulation.

intents.q: Hand a project over to someone else

cmds.n: Moves the repository with its issues, pull requests, and history intact.
Before handing over: a README that explains running and deploying it, CODEOWNERS updated, secrets rotated, and any personal tokens revoked.

variants.undo: The new owner can transfer it back

intents.q: Contribute to a project without writing code

cmds.c: Edit this file, on any GitHub page
cmds.n: The pencil icon forks, branches, and opens a pull request in one flow. Documentation fixes are how most maintainers meet their future contributors.
Triage, reproduction steps, and translations count too, and are often scarcer than code.

intents.q: Review a pull request written with AI assistance

cmds.n: Run it. Generated code compiles and reads well far more often than it is correct, so execution and tests carry the review.
Check the parts models get wrong: error paths, edge cases, invented APIs, and dependencies nobody vetted. Authorship does not change the standard, only where you look first.

intents.q: One repository holding several languages

cmds.n: Combine each ecosystem's rules, scoped by folder, rather than one sprawling file at the root.
Give each stack its own workflow so a frontend change does not run the Python suite.

intents.q: Change the license of an existing project

cmds.n: Contributors hold copyright on their commits, so a relicense usually needs their agreement. This is the list of people to ask.

cmds.c: git add LICENSE && git commit -m "Relicense under Apache-2.0"
cmds.n: The new license applies from that commit forward. Versions already published under the old terms stay available under them permanently.

variants.undo: Commit the old license back, for future versions only

intents.q: Require a CLA or a DCO from contributors

cmds.n: Contributors attest with a Signed-off-by line. A bot can enforce it on pull requests. Enough for most projects.
A signed agreement, sometimes assigning rights to a foundation or company. It raises the barrier for casual contributors, so require it only when legal counsel does.

intents.q: Keep copyright headers current

cmds.n: Per-file years drift and create noisy diffs. A single year of first publication, or none at all, is the modern practice; the LICENSE file carries the real terms.
Where a header is mandated, generate it from history rather than editing by hand.

intents.q: Publish a security advisory for my project

cmds.n: Draft privately, collaborate in a temporary private fork, and request a CVE from GitHub at no cost.
On release, Dependabot alerts every downstream project automatically. Publishing before the fix ships helps attackers, not users.

variants.undo: Advisories can be withdrawn, but assume the disclosure is permanent

intents.q: Get an automated first-pass review

cmds.c: Reviewers -> Copilot, on the pull request
cmds.n: It comments on obvious defects and style before a human looks, which raises the floor of what reaches your reviewers.
Machine review does not count toward required approvals, and should not: judgement about whether a change is right remains human work.

intents.q: Set what everyone in the organization can see

cmds.c: Organization -> Settings -> Member privileges -> Base permissions
cmds.n: Read gives every member visibility into all repositories, which suits open internal cultures. None forces explicit grants, which suits regulated ones.
Pair it with who may create repositories and who may make them public.

variants.undo: Change the setting back; explicit grants survive

intents.q: Run open source practices inside a company

cmds.n: On an enterprise account, internal repositories are visible to every member but nobody outside. The default home for shared internal libraries.

cmds.c: git switch -c fix/<topic> && gh pr create
cmds.n: Then treat other teams as contributors: CODEOWNERS, a CONTRIBUTING file, and pull requests instead of tickets.

intents.q: I committed and pushed to the wrong repository

cmds.n: Export your commits from the wrong repository.
Apply them in the right one, keeping author and message.

variants.undo: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD in the correct repository

cmds.n: On a shared repository, revert rather than rewrite. If the push was private and seconds old, git reset --hard and a force push are acceptable.

intents.q: Prove when I wrote something

cmds.n: Commit dates are self-reported and editable, so an unsigned date proves little. A signed commit ties content to your key.
A push to a hosted repository creates a third-party record with its own timestamp, which is far stronger evidence than local history alone.

intents.q: It passes locally but fails in CI

cmds.n: An uncommitted or ignored file that CI never sees is the most common cause by far.
Confirm CI ran the commit you think it did, not a merge preview of an older base.
Then compare versions, environment variables, timezone, and case sensitivity: Linux runners are case-sensitive where Windows and macOS are not.

intents.q: A teammate's push overwrote my commits
aka: someone force pushed over my work
my commits vanished from the branch

cmds.n: Your clone still holds them. Find the hash from before their push and branch it: git branch rescue <hash>.
Publish the rescue branch before anything else touches the repository.
The technical fix. The social fix is agreeing that shared branches are never rewritten.

intents.q: Leave a team or company cleanly

cmds.n: Push everything unfinished first, then remove your tokens, SSH keys, and any deploy keys you created.
If work commits used a company address, keep that address on your account or add a mailmap entry, or your contribution history goes blank.

variants.undo: Access can be regranted; contribution history cannot be rebuilt after the account link breaks

intents.q: Name a repository well

cmds.n: Lowercase, hyphens, and descriptive rather than clever. The name appears in URLs, clone commands, and search results, so searchable beats witty.
Renaming later works and redirects, but every clone, badge, and bookmark carries the old name until updated.

variants.undo: Rename back while the old name is unclaimed

intents.q: Issue, discussion, or pull request

cmds.n: Something is broken or must be built: a unit of work with a resolution.
You already have the change: propose it directly, which maintainers usually prefer to a proposal issue.
A question, an idea, or anything without an obvious owner.

variants.undo: Issues convert to discussions and back

intents.q: Handle issues nobody will ever fix

cmds.n: Closing honestly is kinder than leaving a request open for years. Not planned records the decision without implying it was fixed.
Review by date, and prefer a human sweep to an automatic stale bot, which mostly annoys the people who reported real bugs.

intents.q: Share maintenance so the project survives me

cmds.n: Grant merge rights to whoever already reviews well. A project with one person holding every permission dies with their interest.
Document decisions in CONTRIBUTING and MAINTAINERS files so authority does not live only in your head.

intents.q: Collapse an entire history into one commit
aka: start history over but keep files

cmds.n: A branch with no parent, carrying your current files.
One commit holding everything as it stands today.
Replaces published history entirely. Every clone and open pull request breaks, so do this only on a repository nobody else uses.

variants.undo: Only from another clone that still has the old history

intents.q: Break one big commit into several

cmds.n: Mark the commit edit, so the rebase stops with it applied.
Uncommit it, leaving the changes in the working tree.
Commit in pieces, then git rebase --continue.

variants.undo: git rebase --abort mid-way, git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD after

intents.q: origin/main and main are different things

cmds.n: main is yours to move; origin/main is a cached note of where the server was at your last fetch. Neither updates the other by itself.
Refreshes the cached note only. Your branch and files move only when you merge, rebase, or reset.

intents.q: I amended a commit that was already pushed

cmds.n: Replaces the remote commit and refuses if someone else pushed meanwhile, which plain --force would trample.

variants.undo: Push the original hash back from your reflog

cmds.c: git revert <hash> or a new commit
cmds.n: Leave the published commit alone. Anyone who pulled would otherwise get a confusing duplicate history.

intents.q: clean or reset, which one do I need
aka: remove new files vs undo changes

cmds.n: Or reset --hard for the whole tree: both act on files Git already knows.

variants.undo: Only through the reflog if the content was ever committed or staged

cmds.n: Only clean touches untracked files. Rehearse with -n first, because Git holds no copy of them at all.

intents.q: Why my fork needs two remotes
aka: which remote do i pull from

cmds.n: origin is your fork, the only place you can push. upstream is the original, which you pull from but never push to.

cmds.c: git fetch upstream && git merge upstream/main
cmds.n: That split is why syncing a fork takes two remotes rather than one.

intents.q: Show how active a project is

cmds.n: Total commits on this branch. git rev-list --count --since="1 month ago" HEAD narrows it to recent activity, which is the more honest number.
Weekly activity over time, and a last-commit badge from shields.io says more to visitors than a total ever will.

intents.q: Stop release tags from being moved or deleted

cmds.n: Match a pattern like v* and block deletions and updates. Published tags are promises; this keeps them.
Creating new tags still works; only moving or deleting existing ones is refused.

intents.q: Open a pull request before writing the code

cmds.n: An empty commit gives the branch something to push, so the pull request exists as a place to argue about the plan.
Draft status makes the intent obvious and keeps the merge button out of reach until the work is real.

intents.q: Try a colleague's branch on my machine

cmds.n: Git creates a local branch tracking theirs automatically.

variants.undo: git switch - and delete the local branch

cmds.n: The simplest path when a pull request exists. Otherwise add their fork as a remote and fetch from it.

variants.undo: git switch - and remove the remote

intents.q: My editor keeps adding files to the repository

cmds.n: Add .idea/ and .vscode/ there once and no repository of yours ever sees them again, without imposing your editor choice on anyone.
When they were already committed. Share only the parts of editor config that genuinely help everyone.

intents.q: See every version of one file at once

cmds.n: Every commit that touched it, with the patch, following renames.
The index version: hashes to feed into git show <hash>:<path> when you want a specific one.

intents.q: Pass a built file from one job to the next

cmds.n: Jobs run on separate machines with nothing shared, so the file must be uploaded.
In the later job, with needs: pointing at the earlier one. Build once and deploy the same bytes rather than rebuilding.

intents.q: GitHub says my repository is too large

cmds.n: Almost always a handful of large binaries committed over time, not the source.
Rewrites history without them, then force-push. Everyone must reclone.
Or move them to LFS, which keeps them available while shrinking the pack.

variants.undo: Only from a clone with the old history

intents.q: Update my pull request branch with the latest main
aka: pr out of date with main

cmds.n: Or the Update branch button on the pull request. Adds a merge commit and never rewrites what reviewers already read.
Tidier history, but review comments can detach from rewritten commits. Prefer it before review starts, not during.

variants.undo: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD, then force-push again

intents.q: Audit who approved a change

cmds.c: gh pr view <number> --json reviews --jq ".reviews[] | {who: .author.login, state: .state, when: .submittedAt}"
cmds.n: Every review with its verdict and timestamp, which is what audits ask for.
Start from a commit and find the pull request that carried it, then read its approvals.

intents.q: My first pull request to a stranger's project

cmds.n: Read it first: most rejections are process mismatches, not code judgements. Start with something small enough that review is quick.
Say what changed and why in two sentences. Silence for a week is normal on volunteer projects and is not a verdict on your work.

intents.q: A maintainer asked me to rebase or squash

cmds.c: git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main
cmds.n: Resolve any conflicts as they appear, then git push --force-with-lease to your fork; the pull request updates itself.

variants.undo: git rebase --abort mid-way, git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD after

cmds.n: Everything becomes a single commit with a fresh message. Faster than an interactive rebase when the target is one commit.

intents.q: Keep working while GitHub is down

cmds.n: Git is local, so committing, branching, merging, and reading history all keep working. Only push, pull, and the website need the service.
For a long outage, hand work to a colleague as a bundle, or push to a second remote.

intents.q: Recover a file someone deleted, from the website

cmds.n: The path's history still resolves after deletion. Open the last commit before it went, then view the file at that commit and copy or restore it.
Or locate the deleting commit locally and restore from its parent.

intents.q: Branch, tag, or release for a version

cmds.n: A tag names one commit permanently: the version itself.
A branch is for continuing work on that line, such as patches for 2.1 after 2.2 ships.
A release is the page, notes, and downloads wrapped around the tag.

variants.undo: Each has its own delete command

intents.q: Clone is stuck at resolving deltas

cmds.n: Delta resolution is local CPU work on a large history. Skipping old file contents avoids most of it.
Shows whether it is transferring or grinding. A shallow clone finishes when a full one will not.

intents.q: Commit without an editor opening

cmds.n: The editor opens only when no message is supplied. Repeat -m for extra paragraphs.
Or read the message from a file, which suits scripts and long bodies.

intents.q: Go back to the branch I was just on

cmds.n: Returns to the previous branch, and again to toggle back.
When you switched several times and lost track, the reflog names every position in order.

intents.q: See both sides of a conflict separately

cmds.n: Your side. :3: is theirs and :1: is the common ancestor, so you can inspect each cleanly instead of reading markers.
Rewrites the markers to include the ancestor, which usually makes the right resolution obvious.

variants.undo: git checkout -m <path> restores the plain conflict

intents.q: Work with a repository that has no commits yet

cmds.n: Before the first commit there is no HEAD, so log, diff, and branch all complain. One commit makes the repository usable.
The branch exists on the remote only once a commit is pushed onto it.

variants.undo: git update-ref -d HEAD removes the only commit

intents.q: Blame a line from the GitHub website

cmds.c: Blame button on any file view
cmds.n: Each line shows the commit that last changed it. Press b as a keyboard shortcut.
Add reformatting commits there and both the site and local blame skip past them to the real author.

intents.q: Pull request checks are stuck as expected

cmds.n: A required check that never runs stays pending forever. Usually its workflow was renamed, skipped by a paths filter, or gated behind first-time approval.
Remove the stale check name, or make the workflow always run and exit early instead of being skipped.

variants.undo: Re-add the requirement once the workflow is fixed

intents.q: Partial clone or shallow clone

cmds.n: Keeps every commit but downloads file contents on demand. log, blame, and bisect all work.

variants.when: You need only the latest state

cmds.n: Smallest and fastest, but history-dependent commands fail. Right for CI, wrong for daily work.

intents.q: Stop notifications from one noisy repository
aka: too many emails from one repo

cmds.n: Silences everything from that repository, including mentions.
Usually better: keep release news and drop the rest. Being a collaborator subscribes you automatically, which is where most floods start.

variants.undo: Set Watch back to Participating and mentions

intents.q: A cherry-pick hit a conflict

cmds.n: Same conflict machinery as a merge: edit the files, stage them.
Completes the pick with the resolution.

variants.when: It conflicts because context is missing

cmds.n: A commit that depends on earlier ones conflicts on its own. Pick the range, or backport the whole series.

intents.q: Keep a tidy history when working alone

cmds.n: Commit fixes marked for a specific earlier commit as you work.
Folds every fixup into its target automatically. Safe on unpushed work, and the tidiest habit for solo history.

intents.q: Someone deleted a file and it was merged
aka: bring back file deleted by teammate

cmds.n: Finds the commit that removed it.
Brings the file back from the commit before, then commit it as a normal change. Reverting the whole merge would undo everything else in it too.

intents.q: Turn TODO comments into tracked work

cmds.n: Searches tracked files only, so build output never floods the list. Add --heading for readable grouping.
A TODO with no issue behind it is a note to nobody. Reference the issue number in the comment so the two stay linked.

intents.q: Search code across all branches and history

cmds.n: Slow on large repositories but exhaustive. Narrow with a path argument.
Finds the commits that added or removed the string, which is usually the real question.

intents.q: Copy someone's changes without their commits

cmds.n: Stages the combined result with no merge commit and no incoming history, ready for you to commit as one change.
Credit the original author in the message or with a Co-authored-by trailer, since the commits themselves are gone.

intents.q: Restrict who can change certain files
aka: only some people edit this file

cmds.n: Git itself has no per-path permissions, so this is enforced by review: owners must approve changes under that path.

cmds.c: Ruleset -> Require review from Code Owners
cmds.n: Without this rule the ownership is advisory only.

variants.undo: Remove the rule or the CODEOWNERS line

intents.q: Start one workflow from another

cmds.n: Runs on the default branch with the earlier run's outcome available, which suits deploy-after-test.
With workflow_dispatch, any job or person can start it with inputs. Simpler to reason about than chaining.

intents.q: Lock a release branch after it ships

cmds.n: Blocks pushes while leaving the branch readable and cloneable, which is what a freeze actually means.
For a permanent record, tag the tip; tags are immutable in practice and protectable by rule.

intents.q: Run a workflow only for version tags

cmds.n: Matches release tags and ignores branches entirely, so nightly or scratch tags do not trigger a release.
Or gate a single job inside a shared workflow when you would rather keep one file.

intents.q: Keep everyone credited after a squash merge

cmds.n: GitHub collects trailers from the squashed commits into the merge commit body, so every contributor keeps credit. Check the message before confirming the merge.
Lists the original authors when you need to add trailers by hand.

intents.q: Review a diff too large for the browser

cmds.n: The full patch locally, where your editor handles what the browser refuses.
Or split the review by path, and ask for the pull request to be broken up: a diff the browser cannot render is usually one a human cannot review either.

intents.q: My branch list disagrees with GitHub
aka: branches show that do not exist

cmds.n: Remote-tracking branches are a cache from your last fetch. Prune drops the ones deleted upstream.
Shows what would go before it goes, when you would rather look first.

variants.undo: Another fetch restores anything still on the server

intents.q: I lost access to my two-factor device

cmds.c: Use a recovery code at sign-in
cmds.n: The codes issued when you enabled two-factor are the primary route back in. A second registered passkey or device also works.
Once back in, regenerate the codes and register a second factor. Without codes or a second device, account recovery is slow and may fail.

intents.q: Fix remotes after a repository was renamed or moved

cmds.n: Old URLs keep working through a redirect, which hides the problem until the old name is reused by someone else.
Update every clone, plus CI configuration, submodule URLs, and badge links.

intents.q: Undo committing node_modules or vendor

cmds.n: Then git rm -r --cached node_modules and commit. New clones are clean; the old copies remain in history.
Only worth it when the repository is painfully large. Everyone must reclone afterwards.

variants.undo: Only from a clone with the old history

intents.q: My history is full of merge branch main commits
aka: merge branch main into main noise

cmds.n: Each pull with local commits creates a merge. Rebasing on pull replays your work on top instead, and the noise stops.
Only on unpushed history. Published merges are noise you live with, not a reason to rewrite a shared branch.

intents.q: Should every task get its own branch

cmds.n: One branch per reviewable unit. Two unrelated changes on one branch force a reviewer to judge both together and block each on the other.
When you notice a second thing mid-work, branch again from main rather than piling it on.

intents.q: I pushed a merge that should not have happened

cmds.n: Undoes the merge as a new commit, safe on a shared branch. Note that re-merging that branch later needs care, since Git considers it already merged.
When the branch is genuinely ready later, revert the revert rather than re-merging.

intents.q: I opened a pull request from main by mistake

cmds.n: Create the branch you should have used; it points at the same commits.
Open a new pull request from it, close the old one, then reset your main back: git switch main && git reset --hard origin/main.

variants.undo: The old branch tip is in the reflog

intents.q: My very first workflow fails immediately

cmds.n: Indentation errors, a missing checkout step, or a runner without your toolchain account for nearly all first failures.
Workflows start with an empty machine: without this step there is no code to build.

intents.q: A secret appeared in workflow logs

cmds.n: Logs may have been read or cached. Rotation is the only real fix; deleting the run is housekeeping.
Then remove the run so the value stops being served.
Masks any computed value, not just declared secrets. Avoid set -x in steps that touch credentials.

intents.q: Know which commit is actually in production

cmds.n: Deployments record the exact commit per environment, which branch names never can.
Without deployment records, tag each release so production is always traceable to a commit.

intents.q: I pushed but GitHub does not show my changes

cmds.n: If this is not your commit, the push went to a different branch or a different remote.
Two remotes, or a fork instead of the original, is the most common explanation.

variants.when: You are looking at the wrong place

cmds.n: The repository page shows the default branch; your commits may be sitting on another branch entirely.

intents.q: Work with people who do not use Git
aka: how do others contribute without git

cmds.c: Edit this file, in the browser
cmds.n: The web editor covers text changes with no tooling at all, and the result is a normal pull request.
For binary assets, let them drop files into an issue or shared folder and commit on their behalf, crediting them with a Co-authored-by trailer.

intents.q: Check a repository before sharing the link

cmds.n: Description, license, and topics are the three fields most often left empty, and all three show on the page.
Then read your own README as a stranger, confirm the default branch builds, and check no secret sits in history.

intents.q: A dependency I rely on was abandoned

cmds.n: Confirm it is actually dormant, then check whether an active fork already exists: the forks page sorts by recent activity.
If you must maintain it, fork, pin your dependency to your fork, and say so in your README. Offer the fixes upstream first.

intents.q: My pull request shows no changes

cmds.n: Empty means the base already contains everything, often because you branched after the work merged, or targeted the wrong base.
Or the commits are still local. A pull request compares what the remote has, never your working tree.

intents.q: Commit generated code or build it in CI

cmds.n: When consumers need it without your toolchain, or the generator is slow or unavailable in CI. Mark it linguist-generated so diffs collapse.
The default: derived files drift from their source and cause conflicts nobody can resolve meaningfully. Add a CI check that regeneration produces no diff.

intents.q: Give my first code review well
aka: how to review code as a junior
what to say in a review

cmds.n: Read for correctness first, then clarity. Questions beat commands: asking why a branch handles the empty case that way finds more bugs than declaring it wrong.
Say what you checked and what you could not judge. An honest partial review is useful; a rubber stamp is not.

intents.q: revert, reset, and restore compared

cmds.n: Files only: throw away working-tree or staged changes. Nothing about history moves.
Moves the branch pointer. Rewrites your local history, so it belongs to unpushed work.
Adds a new commit undoing an old one. The only safe undo for published history.

variants.undo: Each has its own; revert is itself revertible

intents.q: Push several commits at once or one at a time

cmds.n: Push sends every commit the remote lacks, in order, as one operation. There is no cost to batching, and CI runs once rather than per commit.
To publish only up to a point, name the commit. The rest stay local until you push again.

variants.undo: git push --force-with-lease to move the branch back

intents.q: My stash is missing after switching branches

cmds.n: Stashes are global to the repository, not per branch, so switching cannot hide them. An empty list means one was popped or dropped.
A dropped stash lingers as an unreachable commit. Inspect candidates with git show and restore with git stash apply <hash>.

intents.q: A setting is not doing what I expect

cmds.n: Prints the winning value and the file it came from. Local beats global beats system, so a repository setting can quietly override your global one.
Every level that sets it, so you can see what is being overridden.

intents.q: The repository seems to have two separate histories

cmds.n: Two root commits mean two projects were joined with --allow-unrelated-histories, or a branch was created orphaned.
Lists every root commit, which confirms it.
A merge commit connects the two lines from that point forward. Earlier history stays separate, which is honest.

intents.q: A colleague cannot see the repository I shared

cmds.n: GitHub returns 404 rather than 403 for private repositories, so no access looks identical to not existing. Confirm they are invited and accepted.
Lists who actually has access, which settles the question quickly.

intents.q: Read ahead and behind counts correctly

cmds.n: Ahead means commits you have that the remote lacks; behind means the reverse. Both at once is divergence, which needs a merge or rebase, not just a push.
The two numbers directly, for scripts and prompts.

intents.q: My tag is not on the releases page

cmds.n: Tags do not travel with a normal push, which is the usual cause. Push them explicitly or use --follow-tags.
A pushed tag appears under Tags but is not a release until you create one from it.

intents.q: My workflow runs an old version of the code

cmds.n: Compare with your latest commit. On pull_request events the run uses a merge preview, not your branch tip, which explains most confusion.
When a job genuinely needs the branch tip rather than the merge result.

intents.q: Keep two long-lived branches in step

cmds.c: git switch develop && git merge main
cmds.n: Merge one direction consistently, usually from the stable branch into the active one, so the same conflict never gets resolved twice in two places.
Check the gap regularly; a divergence measured in weeks is a project risk, not a chore.

intents.q: Ask the right number of reviewers

cmds.n: One or two people who know the area. Requesting a whole team usually means nobody feels responsible.
Set the floor in a rule rather than by habit, so it holds when everyone is busy.

intents.q: My README is not showing on the repository page

cmds.n: It must be at the repository root, on the default branch, and named README with a recognised extension. A README inside a folder renders only on that folder's page.
Check you are looking at the default branch; a README added on a feature branch shows only there.

intents.q: Only file permissions changed, not content

cmds.n: Mode changes show as mode change lines with no content diff. Common after copying files between filesystems or through Docker.
Stops Git tracking the executable bit locally. Where the bit genuinely matters, set it deliberately with git update-index --chmod=+x <file>.

intents.q: Required reviews block me when I work alone
aka: cannot approve my own pull request

cmds.n: Keep the pull request requirement and status checks, and drop only the approval count. You still get CI and a diff to read before merging.
Adding yourself is the other option, but it removes the discipline the rule was for.

variants.undo: Raise the approval count when the team grows

intents.q: Work with no internet connection

cmds.n: Every clone holds the full history, so committing, branching, merging, searching, and reading logs need no network at all.
Before going offline, fetch everything you might need: other branches, tags, and submodules. Only push and fetch require a connection.

intents.q: Terminal or a graphical client
aka: should i use the command line

cmds.n: Learn the terminal for the model and for anything unusual: every guide, error message, and answer online speaks it.
Use a graphical client for what it does better: staging hunks, reading history, and resolving conflicts side by side. Most people end up using both.

intents.q: Separate repositories per client or project

cmds.n: One private repository per engagement keeps access, history, and handover boundaries clean when the relationship ends.
Set the identity per repository so client work never carries a personal address, or the reverse.

variants.undo: Transfer or archive the repository at handover

intents.q: The repository name I want is taken

cmds.n: Often an old or archived repository of yours holds it. Rename or delete that one, or pick a scoped name.
Names are unique per account, not globally, so an organization or a prefix frees it immediately.

intents.q: Diff a single path across two commits

cmds.n: Any two commits, tags, or branches, limited to that path.
The same comparison in your editor when the patch is hard to read.

intents.q: Recreate a lost repository from a surviving copy

cmds.n: Run it in a clone that has the history. Branches and tags all land in the new repository.
A bundle is a complete repository in one file; clone it, add the new remote, and push.

intents.q: Stop Git opening an editor on every pull

cmds.n: Or set the environment variable GIT_MERGE_AUTOEDIT to no. The prompt exists so you can explain merges into a topic branch.
Rebasing on pull avoids the merge entirely, which removes the prompt and the merge noise together.

intents.q: Format prose so diffs stay readable

cmds.n: Reflowed paragraphs turn a one-word edit into a whole-paragraph diff. Word diff helps, but the real fix is in how you write the file.
Break lines at sentence ends. Rendering is unaffected in Markdown, and every future diff points at the sentence that actually changed.

intents.q: I deleted the wrong repository

cmds.n: Restorable for a limited window with issues and stars intact, unless it was part of a fork network.
Any surviving clone rebuilds the code and history. Issues and pull requests do not come back.

intents.q: What actually happens when I clone
aka: what do i get when cloning

cmds.n: Downloads the full object database, creates a remote named origin, sets up a tracking branch for the default branch, and checks out its files.
Other branches came down too as remote-tracking refs; only one is checked out. Nothing further is downloaded until you fetch.

intents.q: Fix the author on the last commit only

cmds.n: Set the identity first, or the amend repeats the mistake.
Rewrites the last commit with the current identity and keeps the message.

variants.undo: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD, or the reflog after pushing

intents.q: Give someone read-only access
aka: let them see but not push

cmds.n: They can clone, read issues, and open pull requests from a fork, but cannot push.

cmds.c: Settings -> Deploy keys -> Add deploy key
cmds.n: Read-only unless you tick write access, and scoped to this repository alone. The right choice for servers and CI.

intents.q: I keep pushing to the wrong remote

cmds.n: Makes pushes to that remote fail immediately with an obvious message, which is the usual guard on a fork's upstream.
Confirms which URL each remote pushes to; fetch and push can differ.

intents.q: Make force pushing as safe as it can be

cmds.n: Anything listed here is work you are about to erase. Empty output means only your own commits are being replaced.
Refuses unless your clone has seen the remote's current tip, which catches the case plain force-with-lease misses after a background fetch.

variants.undo: Push the previous hash back from the reflog

intents.q: Keep my Git configuration the same everywhere
aka: same git settings on all machines

cmds.n: Keep shared settings in a versioned file and include them, so machine-specific values stay out of the repository.
Conditional includes switch identity and settings by folder, which handles work and personal on one machine.

intents.q: Submodule or published package for shared code

cmds.n: A versioned package is the answer whenever consumers can tolerate release cycles. Dependency tooling handles upgrades, and nobody needs to know your repository layout.
Right when the code must be built from source in step with the parent, or when no registry exists for it. The cost is that every clone and CI job must handle submodules.

variants.undo: git rm <path> and remove the .gitmodules entry

intents.q: My fork of a private repository and who sees it

cmds.n: A fork inherits the upstream's visibility and access, so anyone with access to the original can reach yours. It is not a private workspace.
For genuinely separate work, mirror into a repository you own instead of forking.

intents.q: How large a pull request should be

cmds.n: Review quality falls off sharply past a few hundred changed lines. If the diff is larger, the split is usually obvious: refactor first, behaviour second.
Splitting after the fact is work, but far less than the review it saves.

intents.q: Set up so I can never lose work

cmds.n: Commit early and often: the reflog protects anything committed for about ninety days, and nothing else.
Push at least daily, even to a wip branch. A commit on one machine is not a backup.
Before any risky command, shelve everything, including untracked files.

variants.undo: Each has its own recovery route

intents.q: A pull request was force-pushed mid-review

cmds.c: Compare button on the pull request timeline
cmds.n: GitHub records each force push and offers a diff between the old and new head, so you can review only what changed since your last pass.
Outdated review comments detach from rewritten commits, which is why rebasing mid-review is discouraged rather than forbidden.

intents.q: Make a large repository pleasant for new joiners

cmds.n: Sets up partial clone, sparse checkout, and background maintenance in one command, which is the whole large-repository toolkit.
On an existing clone, scheduled upkeep keeps day-to-day commands fast without changing anyone's workflow.

intents.q: Share work in progress with one person

cmds.n: A pushed branch is visible to anyone with repository access but appears in no pull request list until you open one.
A draft pull request is the clearer signal when you want their eyes but not the team's.

intents.q: Decide what to do with dozens of old branches

cmds.n: Oldest first. Merged branches can go immediately; the rest need a decision, not indefinite storage.
For unmerged work worth keeping, tag it and delete the branch. The history survives without cluttering the list.

variants.undo: Recreate a branch from its archive tag

intents.q: Why checkout was split into switch and restore

cmds.n: Moving between branches. Its own command because that is what checkout was mostly used for.
Changing file contents. Splitting the two removed the classic trap where one careless checkout silently discarded work.

variants.undo: Each has its own; checkout still works for both

intents.q: I committed then immediately spotted a typo
aka: fix commit right after making it

cmds.n: Folds the fix into the commit you just made, message unchanged. The cleanest option while the commit is still private.
A new commit. Rewriting published history for a typo costs everyone more than the extra line in the log.

intents.q: Build on top of an unmerged pull request

cmds.n: Brings their branch down locally.
Branch from it and target your pull request at theirs, so reviewers see only your addition. Retarget to main once theirs merges.

variants.undo: Change the base and rebase onto main

intents.q: Make sure a secret file can never be committed

cmds.n: First line: it never becomes tracked.
Second line, as a pre-commit hook: catches credentials pasted into files that are not ignored.
Third line, on the server, in case the first two are bypassed.

intents.q: Clone one branch and nothing else

cmds.n: Only that branch's history comes down, and fetch stays limited to it afterwards.
To add another branch later without recloning, then fetch.

variants.undo: git remote set-branches origin "*" && git fetch

intents.q: Check whether a specific commit reached main

cmds.n: Every branch holding that exact commit. Add -r for remote branches.
After a squash or rebase the hash changes, so containment fails even though the change shipped. cherry compares by content instead.

intents.q: Find out what a Git command actually did

cmds.n: Every move HEAD made, labelled with the command that caused it: commit, rebase, reset, merge. The first place to look when something surprising happened.
Prints the internal steps. GIT_TRACE_PACKET=1 adds the network conversation, which settles most remote mysteries.

intents.q: Keep a busy repository from descending into chaos

cmds.n: Serialises merges so two independently green pull requests cannot break main together.
Then short branches, one merge method, CODEOWNERS for routing, and automatic branch cleanup. Chaos in busy repositories is nearly always a missing convention rather than too many people.

intents.q: My commit broke the build for everyone

cmds.n: Unblock everyone before diagnosing. Reverting is not an admission of anything; leaving main broken while you think is the actual mistake.

cmds.c: Ruleset -> Require status checks to pass
cmds.n: A commit that reached main without passing CI means the rule is missing, not that someone was careless.

intents.q: Keep my messy commits or squash them

cmds.n: When the commits are a diary of your afternoon: wip, fix, oops. Nobody benefits from bisecting through those.
When each commit is a deliberate, reviewable step. Curated history is genuinely valuable; the mistake is pretending a messy branch qualifies.

intents.q: Find the commit that added a specific line
aka: search for the change that introduced this

cmds.n: Finds commits where the number of occurrences changed: the one that added it, and the one that removed it.
Regular expression matching against the diff itself when the exact string is unknown.

intents.q: Juggle two features without mixing them up

cmds.n: Shelve, switch, deal with the urgent thing, then pop. Label the stash: an unlabelled one is a mystery by Thursday.
Two folders, two branches, no switching at all. Better than stashing when both features are live for days.

intents.q: Which tense and language for commit messages

cmds.c: git commit -m "Add retry to the upload path"
cmds.n: Imperative mood, as if completing the sentence: if applied, this commit will add retry. It matches what Git itself generates for merges and reverts.
Match the project's existing language and style. Consistency matters more than any particular rule.

intents.q: Cut the noise in a repository's history

cmds.n: Bulk reformatting commits stay in history but stop hiding real authorship in blame.
Then agree a formatter so style never lands in a feature commit again.

variants.undo: Remove the file or the config

intents.q: A GitHub link gives 404 but should work
aka: page not found but repo exists

cmds.n: GitHub hides private repositories behind 404 rather than 403, so a missing page usually means wrong account or no access, not a bad link.
Also check for a rename or transfer: redirects stop working once the old name is claimed by someone else.

intents.q: Remove someone's access without breaking things

cmds.n: Their commits stay in history and keep their name: authorship is a record, not a permission.
Then audit what else they set up: deploy keys, webhooks, tokens in CI, and any automation running as them.

intents.q: Keep a changelog current without hating it

cmds.n: Derive notes from merged pull request titles, which makes titles the thing worth reviewing. Nothing extra to maintain.
A hand-written file suits libraries where users need migration notes. Use merge=union in .gitattributes so parallel entries stop conflicting.

intents.q: Put a branch back to how it was yesterday
aka: undo a days worth of commits

cmds.n: Find the last commit from before the change you regret.
On unpushed work. For a shared branch use git revert over the range instead, which undoes the content without rewriting anything.

intents.q: Stop CI wasting minutes on cloning

cmds.n: The default already fetches only one commit, which is right for most jobs.
Only add this when a step genuinely needs history: changelog generation, diff against a base, or version tags. It is the usual cause of slow checkouts.

intents.q: Work out who owns or maintains a repository
aka: who to contact about a repo

cmds.n: The account it belongs to, which is not always who maintains it.
Recent commit volume identifies actual maintainers. CODEOWNERS, MAINTAINERS, and the SECURITY policy name the responsible parties directly.

intents.q: Linear history or merge commits

cmds.n: Every merge must fast-forward, so log reads as one line and bisect is trivial. The cost is rebasing before every merge.
History records what actually happened, including when work happened in parallel. Neither is wrong; consistency within a repository is what matters.

intents.q: One remote over SSH and another over HTTPS
aka: ssh for one remote https for another

cmds.n: Authentication follows the URL scheme, per remote, so mixing them is fine: origin over SSH and a mirror over HTTPS coexist without configuration.
Switch either one at any time. Only the URL decides which credential path is used.

intents.q: Template repository or fork for starting projects

cmds.n: Fresh history, no fork relationship, and the new repository stands alone. Right for boilerplate.
Keeps the link upstream so you can pull improvements and send changes back. Right when you intend to stay connected.

intents.q: Habits that keep credentials out of commits

cmds.n: Read what you are about to commit. The single habit that catches most leaks costs ten seconds.
Staging by hunk makes blind git add . impossible, which is where pasted keys usually slip in.

intents.q: Resolve a conflict in a lockfile

cmds.n: Never hand-merge a lockfile: take one side wholesale.
Then regenerate it from the merged manifest so the result is internally consistent, and commit that.

variants.undo: git checkout -m package-lock.json restores the conflict

intents.q: See what changed since I last pulled
aka: what happened while i was away

cmds.n: Exactly what arrived that you do not have.
Or by time, across every branch, which suits coming back from leave.

intents.q: Deploy one repository to staging and production

cmds.n: One workflow, two jobs, each naming its environment. Environment-scoped secrets and approvals keep the two apart without duplicating the pipeline.
Promote the same artifact rather than rebuilding, so what you tested is what ships.

intents.q: A contributor abandoned their pull request

variants.when: You can push to their branch

cmds.n: With Allow edits by maintainers ticked, finish the work and push back to their fork. They keep authorship.

variants.undo: git reset --hard and force-push their branch back

cmds.c: git fetch <their-fork> <branch> && git switch -c continue/<topic> FETCH_HEAD
cmds.n: Continue on your own branch, credit them with Co-authored-by, and close the original with thanks.

intents.q: Understand what a merge brought in

cmds.n: The commits the merge brought from the other branch, which is usually the real question.
The net effect on the branch that received it.

intents.q: Keep automated branches out of the way

cmds.n: Bots use predictable prefixes, so listing and filtering them is easy.
With automatic deletion on merge, bot branches clean themselves up and never accumulate.

intents.q: Test exactly what I am about to commit

cmds.n: Shelves everything except what is staged, so the working tree matches the commit you are about to make.
Run the tests, commit if green, then restore the rest. This catches the classic case where a commit passes only because of unstaged work.

variants.undo: git stash pop restores the shelf

intents.q: Do I need Projects or are Issues enough
aka: when to add a project board

cmds.n: For a solo or small project, labels, milestones, and a saved search do everything a board would.
Add a board when work spans repositories, needs custom fields like priority or size, or several people need one shared view.

variants.undo: Delete the project; issues are untouched

intents.q: Take one file from another branch without merging

cmds.n: That file becomes main's version, staged for review. Nothing else about the branches changes.
Check the result before committing; taking a file wholesale can quietly drop your own work in it.

intents.q: Somewhere to keep half-finished experiments

cmds.n: One private repository with a folder per experiment beats twenty abandoned public ones, and keeps your profile honest.
For a single file, a secret gist is lighter still and is a real repository underneath.

intents.q: I cloned a project and cannot push to it

cmds.n: Cloning grants no write access. Contributions go through your own fork, then a pull request.
If you should have access, check you cloned the right repository and are authenticated as the right account.

intents.q: What origin/HEAD points at
aka: why is there an origin head

cmds.n: A local note of the remote's default branch, set at clone time. It is why plain git log origin works.
Refresh it after the default branch is renamed, which is when it usually goes stale or breaks.

intents.q: A rebase hits the same conflict on every commit

cmds.n: Records each resolution and replays it when the same conflict reappears, which is exactly this situation.
A merge resolves the conflict once instead of once per commit. When a rebase turns into a slog, merging is the pragmatic answer.

intents.q: Conflicts appear after squashing

cmds.n: Squashing collapses intermediate steps, so a conflict Git previously resolved in stages now lands all at once. Backing out costs nothing.

cmds.c: git merge main && git rebase -i main
cmds.n: Update first, resolve against current main, then squash. Order matters more than technique here.

intents.q: Add CI to a project that never had it

cmds.n: Start with the smallest honest check, even just that the project builds. A green pipeline you trust beats a comprehensive one everyone ignores.
Make it required only once it is reliable, or the first flake teaches the team to bypass rules.

intents.q: I inherited a repository with terrible history
aka: messy history i did not create

cmds.n: Leave it alone. Rewriting inherited history breaks every clone and fork for a cosmetic gain, and the old commits still tell you why the code is the way it is.
Improve what you can non-destructively: ignore-revs for noise, better messages going forward, and a CONTRIBUTING file that sets the new standard.

intents.q: Cherry-pick applied but produced nothing

cmds.n: An equals sign marks commits already present by content, which is why the pick had nothing to do.
Skip it and move on. Use --allow-empty only when you want the empty commit recorded deliberately.

intents.q: Git keeps changing my line endings

cmds.n: Marks the file as never converted, whatever anyone's autocrlf setting is. Correct for binaries and for scripts that must keep exact bytes.

cmds.c:
printf '* text=auto
*.sh text eol=lf
*.bat text eol=crlf
' >> .gitattributes
cmds.n: Committed rules beat per-developer config, and end the argument permanently.

intents.q: I opened a pull request against the wrong repository

cmds.n: The base repository cannot be changed after opening, only the base branch. Close it and apologise briefly; it happens constantly with forks.
The same branch works for the new pull request, so nothing is lost.

variants.undo: Reopen the closed pull request if it was right after all

intents.q: What the plus and colon in a refspec mean

cmds.n: Reads as source:destination. The leading plus allows non-fast-forward updates of the local copy, which is why a force-pushed remote branch still fetches cleanly.
Writing it out explicitly is occasionally useful for fetching one branch into a specific local ref.

intents.q: Inspect what a clone was set up with

cmds.n: Remotes, fetch refspecs, filters, and any tool-written settings. Shows at a glance whether the clone is shallow, single-branch, or partial.
The one thing config does not spell out plainly.

intents.q: Remove a tag from every clone

cmds.n: Both halves are needed, or a later fetch restores the local tag from the remote.
Other people must run this, since normal fetches never delete tags. That is why deleting a published tag is disruptive.

variants.undo: git tag <tag> <hash> and push it again

intents.q: Why my pull created a merge commit

cmds.n: You had local commits and the remote had others, so pull merged the two lines. With no local commits it would have fast-forwarded silently.
Rebasing on pull replays your commits on top instead, which keeps the line straight.

variants.undo: git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD if not pushed

intents.q: Keep my local branch list manageable

cmds.c: git fetch --prune && git branch -vv | grep ": gone]"
cmds.n: Branches whose remote is gone are almost always finished work; delete them with -d, which refuses anything unmerged.
Then judge the rest by recency. A branch you cannot remember the purpose of is a candidate for an archive tag.

variants.undo: Recreate from the reflog or archive tag

intents.q: Search only my own repositories

cmds.n: Scopes the search to your account, including private repositories you can read.
When you know which clone it is in, local grep is faster and works offline.

intents.q: A rebase went wrong and I want out

cmds.n: Returns the branch exactly to where it started, whatever state the rebase reached.
ORIG_HEAD holds the pre-rebase tip. If it has since moved, git reflog names the same commit.

intents.q: Commit a large text file sensibly

cmds.n: Text compresses and diffs well, so a few megabytes is fine and worth versioning. The problem is churn: a file rewritten wholesale every commit grows history fast.
Past tens of megabytes, or when it changes constantly, route it to LFS or out of the repository entirely.

intents.q: I committed on main but wanted a branch
aka: commit on wrong branch move it
move last commit to a new branch

cmds.n: The new branch carries the commits with it, since a branch is only a label.

cmds.c: git switch main && git reset --hard origin/main
cmds.n: Then put main back where the remote has it. The work is safe on the new branch.
On a shared main, revert rather than rewrite, then re-apply the change through a branch and a pull request.

intents.q: Check a repository's merge and branch settings

cmds.n: Default branch, permitted merge methods, and whether branches auto-delete, in one call.
The rules that will block a push before you discover them the hard way.

intents.q: Run a Git command with different settings once

cmds.n: The -c flag applies a setting to that command alone, leaving all config files untouched.
Handy in scripts and one-off diagnostics where you do not want to change anyone's setup.

intents.q: Convert a submodule back into normal files

cmds.n: Removes the submodule registration while leaving the files on disk.
Delete the inner repository so the files become ordinary tracked content, then commit. Their separate history is not preserved.

variants.undo: Re-add the submodule from its URL

intents.q: git status takes seconds to run

cmds.n: A filesystem monitor stops Git rescanning every file. The single biggest win on large working trees.
Caches untracked-file scanning too. On Windows, excluding the repository from antivirus scanning often matters more than either setting.

intents.q: Git keeps asking for my username on every push

cmds.n: On Windows, Git Credential Manager stores the token securely. On macOS use osxkeychain; on Linux, libsecret.
Signing in with the CLI configures the helper for you, which is the shortest path.

intents.q: Merge one branch into several at once

cmds.c: git switch develop && git merge feature
cmds.n: Merge separately into each target. There is no multi-target merge, and cherry-picking instead would duplicate the commits.

cmds.c: git switch main && git merge develop
cmds.n: Where the branches themselves are related, merging along the chain keeps one line of ancestry rather than three.

intents.q: Work out what access I actually have
aka: can i push to this repo

cmds.n: Your effective admin, push, and pull flags for that repository, whatever the path that granted them.
Confirms which account you are acting as, which is the usual surprise when permissions look wrong.

intents.q: Restore one line without touching the rest of the file

cmds.n: Walks the file hunk by hunk, discarding only what you accept. Press s to split a hunk down to the line you want.
Read the diff first so you know which hunk holds the line.

intents.q: Tag a release I forgot to tag

cmds.n: Any commit can be tagged at any time. The tag's own date is today, which is honest and rarely matters.
Then create the release from it if you need notes and downloads.

variants.undo: git tag -d v1.4.0 && git push origin --delete v1.4.0

intents.q: Judge whether a stranger's pull request is safe to run

cmds.n: Read the whole diff first, especially workflow files, build scripts, and new dependencies. Those are where a hostile pull request hides, not in the feature code.
A change to .github/workflows from a first-time contributor deserves particular attention.

intents.q: My fork says it is behind by dozens of commits

cmds.n: Behind simply means upstream moved on; nothing is wrong with your fork. Syncing fast-forwards it when you have no conflicting commits.

cmds.c: git fetch upstream && git merge upstream/main
cmds.n: With your own commits on the branch, merge or rebase instead, which the sync button will refuse to guess at.

intents.q: Share code with someone who has no GitHub account
aka: send code to someone without github

cmds.n: Anyone can read, clone, and download a ZIP without an account. Only interaction needs one.
A single file holding the whole repository, sendable by any means. Or export a snapshot with git archive when history should not travel.

intents.q: Summarise what happened in a repository this month

cmds.n: Who committed and how much, grouped by author.
Merged pull requests read better than raw commits for a summary, since each is a complete change.

intents.q: What to learn in my first week with Git

cmds.n: Status, add, commit, and log. Nothing else. Get comfortable making and reading commits before anything can go wrong.
Branching, pushing, and pull requests. Add reflog last, as the safety net that makes experimentation safe.

intents.q: Leave my work in a safe state before time off

cmds.n: Push every branch, even unfinished ones. Nothing useful should exist only on your machine while you are away.
Open drafts with a note on where you got to, so a colleague can pick it up without archaeology.

intents.q: Catch up after two weeks away

cmds.c: git fetch --all --prune && git log --oneline --since="2 weeks ago" --all
cmds.n: Everything that landed, across branches, in one list.
Merged pull requests read better than raw commits, and their descriptions explain intent.

intents.q: When to stop fighting Git and ask
aka: when to give up on a git problem

cmds.n: Before asking, freeze the state so nothing changes while you explain it. Half of Git problems are solved by describing them precisely.
When a repository is genuinely tangled and the work is pushed, a fresh clone costs minutes and beats an hour of surgery.

intents.q: Set up a repository for a hackathon

cmds.n: Skip ceremony: no rulesets, no required reviews. Everyone pushes to main and communicates out loud.
The one discipline worth keeping is pulling before pushing, which prevents the classic hackathon force-push disaster.

variants.undo: Add protection later if the project survives

intents.q: Move a team off shared folders onto Git

cmds.c: git init && git add . && git commit -m "Import current state"
cmds.n: Start with the code as it is today. Nobody adopts a tool while also being told their history was wrong.
Then teach the smallest loop that works: pull, edit, commit, push. Branches and reviews come once the habit exists.

variants.undo: The folder keeps working exactly as before

intents.q: What a good commit history looks like

cmds.n: Each line should say what changed and why it was needed. If a stranger cannot follow the story, the history is decoration rather than documentation.
The practical test: can you bisect it. That requires every commit to build and to contain one idea.

intents.q: Set a project up to outlive my involvement

cmds.n: A permissive license, documented setup, and a build anyone can run are what let others continue. Undocumented knowledge dies with your interest.
Grant a second person merge rights while you still care, and say plainly in the README what the project's status is.

variants.undo: Archive the repository if nobody takes it on

intents.q: Use Git safely inside a script

cmds.n: Guard first, so the script never operates on the wrong folder.
Silence interactive advice, use plumbing output like --porcelain, and never assume a branch name.

intents.q: Keep badges honest

cmds.n: Pin the branch, or the badge reports whatever ran last, including a branch nobody uses.
A badge that never goes red is usually measuring nothing. Check what the workflow actually asserts.

intents.q: Public or private for a new project

cmds.n: Private costs nothing and can be opened later. Going the other way loses stars, forks, and any secret already published.
When the work is meant to be found, cited, or contributed to. Add the license from the first commit or nobody may legally use it.

variants.undo: Going private later drops stars and detaches forks

intents.q: Break the habit of force pushing

cmds.n: If you must force, make the safe form the easy one, so the dangerous form takes deliberate effort.
On anything shared, the honest fix is a new commit. Force pushing is for your own unpublished branches and almost nothing else.

intents.q: Reconstruct everything I did today
aka: what did i do today git

cmds.n: Every checkout, commit, rebase, and reset in order, including work on branches you have since left.
The committed subset, across every branch, for a standup or a timesheet.

intents.q: Decide which pull requests to review first

cmds.c: gh search prs --review-requested=@me --state open --sort created --order asc
cmds.n: Oldest first stops anyone being blocked for days. Small pull requests before large ones keeps the queue moving.
Skip drafts: they are not asking for your time yet.

intents.q: What breaks when I rename the default branch
aka: what happens when renaming default branch

cmds.n: GitHub retargets open pull requests and redirects most links. What it cannot fix is anything outside the repository.

cmds.n: Annotated tags reachable from what you push now travel with it, which is nearly always what you meant.
The one-off form. Lightweight tags are deliberately excluded, since those are usually private bookmarks.

aka: remove from commit keep on disk

cmds.n: Leaves the file untouched on disk and out of the next commit.
Uncommit, drop that path from the staging area, and commit the rest.

aka: just my commits on this branch

cmds.n: Only what this branch adds on top of main, which is exactly what a reviewer will see.
On main itself, this hides commits that arrived inside merges and shows the release-level story.

intents.q: Catch trailing whitespace before it lands

cmds.n: Reports trailing whitespace and space-before-tab in what you are about to commit. Exits non-zero, so it works as a hook.
When applying someone else's patch, this cleans the damage rather than importing it.

intents.q: The repository has no default branch set

cmds.n: A repository with no commits has no default branch yet; the first pushed branch becomes it.
With several branches and none marked default, set it explicitly or clones will not know what to check out.

intents.q: Two people editing the same file all day
aka: we keep editing the same file

cmds.n: Sync hourly rather than daily: small overlaps resolve trivially, whole-day divergence does not.

A file two people must edit constantly is usually doing too many jobs. Splitting it removes the conflict permanently.

intents.q: I closed the terminal during a rebase

cmds.n: Git keeps the rebase state on disk, so it survives a closed terminal or a reboot and tells you exactly where it stopped.
Pick up where you left off, or git rebase --abort to return to the starting point cleanly.

intents.q: See who forked or copied my project

cmds.n: Forks with their last activity, which separates active derivatives from abandoned copies.
Shows which forks carry commits you do not have, occasionally worth pulling back.

intents.q: Clean up a branch without the terminal

cmds.n: Squash on merge does the cleanup for you, which is why most teams never rewrite branches by hand at all.

intents.q: Find commits not on any branch

cmds.n: Lists dangling commits: leftovers of resets, deleted branches, and abandoned rebases. Often exactly the work you thought was gone.
The reflog view is friendlier: it shows where each was and when, so you can recognise the one you want.

cmds.n: The file is still on disk, so adding it re-tracks it. If it is now ignored, git add -f overrides the rule.

intents.q: A repository with a hundred thousand commits

cmds.n: Precomputes commit relationships, which is what makes log and blame fast on enormous histories.
Then let scheduled maintenance keep it current. Depth of history costs far less than size of files.

The whole working tree regardless of where you stand. git status before committing settles any doubt.

intents.q: My branch vanished after merging

cmds.n: With automatic deletion on merge, the remote branch goes and your local copy is marked gone at the next prune. Expected behaviour, not a loss.

cmds.n: Accepts the generated list as-is, which is exactly what you want when fixup commits already say what to fold.
Scripted edits to the list are possible, though usually more trouble than doing it by hand.

intents.q: GitHub shows the wrong language for my project
aka: github thinks my repo is html

cmds.n: Vendored, generated, and documentation paths skew the bar. Marking them corrects it within a day.
Or override the detected language outright for specific paths.

intents.q: Handle a hostile issue or comment

cmds.n: Locking stops the thread without deleting the record. Hide individual comments as off-topic or abusive rather than arguing.
Block repeat offenders and report abuse. Maintainers owe nobody unpaid emotional labour.

intents.q: Keep history when splitting a file in two

cmds.n: Move first, in its own commit, so Git records the rename cleanly.
Then extract the second file in the next commit. The -C flags follow code moved between files, which is how blame survives the split.

intents.q: Keep a mirror repository automatically in sync

cmds.n: A nightly workflow that fetches and pushes --mirror keeps a second host current without anyone remembering.
Mirror pushes replace refs wholesale, so point them only at a repository that exists to be a mirror.

intents.q: The diff shows the entire file as changed

cmds.n: Every line added and removed at once means the file was rewritten wholesale: CRLF conversion, an encoding change, or a reformat.
If ignoring whitespace collapses the diff to nothing, formatting is the whole story.

intents.q: CI fails randomly on the same commit

cmds.n: A pass on rerun with no code change means the test is unreliable, not the commit.

intents.q: Version several packages in one repository

cmds.n: Prefix tags with the package name so each can move independently and git describe stays meaningful per package.
Then release tooling filters by prefix to find each package's latest version.

intents.q: Is detached HEAD dangerous

cmds.n: Not dangerous by itself: you are simply standing on a commit rather than a branch. Looking around, building, and testing are all fine.
